questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Federalism as a division of sovereignty
questions.learningObjective: Identify which level of government holds the listed power
questions.stem: A reference table lists powers and the level of government exercising each. For the row describing a direct income tax on individuals, which level holds the power?

options.text: Whichever level shows the largest collections in the revenue column of the table
options.misconception: reads a table of amounts as a grant of legal power

options.text: The state government, because states retain the power to tax residents inside their borders
options.misconception: treats collected revenue as proof of taxing authority

options.text: The local government, since a city may levy an income tax with the approval of its voters
options.misconception: believes local taxing is a separate sovereign power

options.text: The national government, since the constitution names direct taxation of individuals as a national power

questions.explanation: Direct taxation of individuals sits with the national government, so that table row belongs there. The other options confuse money raised with the power to impose the tax.
questions.hint: Ask which level the constitution names for this power.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Ambiguity of an enumerated list with a reservation
questions.learningObjective: Resolve an unlisted power by reading the reservation clause
questions.stem: A statute table lists powers granted to the national government and then notes that powers not granted remain with the states or the people. For an unlisted item, who holds the power?

options.text: The national government, because silence in the list lets it act wherever any listed power reaches
options.misconception: reads silence as an open-ended grant of power

options.text: The states and the people, because a reservation clause settles the case for unlisted powers
options.misconception: confuses the reservation with a rule of necessity

options.text: The courts alone, because an unclear statute must always be resolved by the judiciary
options.misconception: thinks courts decide every ambiguity by default

options.text: The states and the people, because an item not named in the list falls outside national authority

questions.explanation: The reserving clause assigns unlisted powers to the states and the people, so the unlisted row follows from the text. Treating silence as a grant of power inverts what the clause does.
questions.hint: The final clause of the table resolves the gap.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Implied powers and incidental authority
questions.learningObjective: Select the programme step supported as implied
questions.stem: A programme table lists data collection, standard setting, and certificate issuance, but the statute authorising the programme names only the certification power. Which step is most defensible as implied?

options.text: Setting numerical standards for every industry, because programmes need benchmarks
options.misconception: assumes implied power reaches any useful measure

options.text: Regulating an unrelated trade entirely, because it touches the same industry
options.misconception: confuses a related subject with an implied power

options.text: Levying a new tax to fund inspectors, because funding is always implied
options.misconception: treats implied authority as covering revenue measures

options.text: Collecting the data needed to issue the certificates the statute does authorise

questions.explanation: Implied power covers the steps needed to carry out the power that was granted, and data collection serves certification. The other options reach beyond the programme's authorised end.
questions.hint: Ask which step is necessary to complete the granted power.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Concurrent power and a national floor
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a national floor from a ceiling on state action
questions.stem: A table sets one national minimum standard and the stricter rules adopted by several states for the same activity. Which statement best describes the legal position?

options.text: Only the national minimum applies, because any stricter state rule is invalid
options.misconception: assumes a federal floor suppresses stricter state rules

options.text: Both apply, because a national floor sets a minimum that states may exceed
options.misconception: confuses the floor with a ceiling on state standard setting

options.text: Only the stricter state rules apply, because states may set any standard they prefer
options.misconception: ignores the binding national minimum

options.text: The two standards operate together, since a state may exceed but not fall below the floor

questions.explanation: A national floor establishes a minimum both levels must meet, so the state rules may be stricter but cannot undercut the floor. Treating the floor as a ceiling misdescribes concurrency.
questions.hint: Ask whether a state rule may go below the listed minimum.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Scope of the commerce power
questions.learningObjective: Apply the interstate movement test to the tabulated lines

stimulus.body: A table lists three lines of activity with their annual dollar volume: freight carried between states, purely local retail sales, and goods entering a single state from abroad. The analyst marks the second line as beyond the reach of the commerce power.

questions.stem: Using the table, which statement best explains why the analyst treats the two flagged lines differently from the freight line?

options.text: Only activity with a substantial effect on interstate commerce can reach the commerce power
options.misconception: treats commerce power as covering all measurable activity

options.text: The freight line involves movement across state lines, while the local and import lines do not
The import line is excluded because foreign commerce is reserved to the states
options.misconception: believes foreign trade is a state power

options.text: The local line is excluded because individuals never count as commerce
options.misconception: reads commerce as covering only business entities

questions.explanation: The freight line shows the interstate movement that anchors the commerce power, while the other lines lack it. Counting every economic effect as commerce overstates the power.
questions.hint: Look for the row that shows goods crossing a border.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Taxing and spending as separate authorities
questions.learningObjective: Separate the taxing authority from the spending authority
questions.stem: A spending table lists grants, tax credits, and a direct levy on individuals, with each row labelled by the authority relied on. Which row rests on the taxing power rather than the spending power?

options.text: The row of annual block grants to states for hospital construction
options.misconception: treats a grant of money as an exercise of taxing power

options.text: The row of matching funds paid to states that meet maintenance standards
options.misconception: assumes matching money is a levy rather than a grant

options.text: The row of a direct levy on the earnings of individuals
The row of tax credits for installing solar equipment
options.misconception: confuses a credit with a direct levy

questions.explanation: The taxing power reaches direct levies on individuals, so the direct levy row rests on it. Grants, credits, and matching payments are spending measures that depend on money already collected.
questions.hint: Ask which row raises money rather than paying it out.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Regulating individuals against commanding a state
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish rules aimed at individuals from rules commanding states
questions.stem: A table compares two federal rules: one forbids a named practice for every covered individual, and one orders a state agency to inspect covered facilities. First identify which rule regulates individuals directly, then state the legal difference.

options.text: Both are the same, because the national government may command anyone it regulates
options.misconception: conflates regulating people with compelling states

options.text: The inspection order is the individual rule, because it reaches facilities rather than people
options.misconception: thinks a command to a state targets individuals

options.text: Neither rule is valid, because only the states may regulate local activity
options.misconception: denies any federal reach over individuals

options.text: The prohibition regulates individuals directly; the order binds a state officer to act

questions.explanation: The two rules differ in who must obey: the prohibition binds individuals directly, while the order binds a state officer. Treating them as equivalent obscures the difference between the two.
questions.hint: Ask who each rule requires to act.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Express preemption
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of an express preemption clause
questions.stem: A statutory table includes a column for preemption clauses. One row states that the listed federal rule displaces any contrary state or local requirement on the same subject. What does that clause establish?

options.text: That the national government may act wherever any listed power reaches
options.misconception: reads silence as an open-ended grant of power

options.text: That no state may ever regulate the subject again, even in areas the rule leaves open
options.misconception: reads a field clause as a ban on all future state action

options.text: That Congress intended federal law to control the field it occupies on that subject
That the state law survives but loses funding whenever the federal rule is enforced
options.misconception: mistakes funding conditions for a preemption rule

questions.explanation: The clause tells courts to apply federal law on the subject it occupies, which is the signature of field preemption. The other readings confuse field displacement with conflict tests.
questions.hint: Ask what the clause directs courts to apply.

questions.topic: Federalism as a division of sovereignty
questions.learningObjective: Characterise sovereignty as divided between two levels
questions.stem: While reviewing a table of powers and the level exercising each, a student notes that a state legislature writes the rules for its own courts. Which observation best reflects the division of sovereignty?

options.text: Each level holds powers that are not the other's, and the two sets overlap in places
Only the national level holds sovereign power; state authority is borrowed and revocable
options.misconception: treats state sovereignty as a revocable grant

options.text: State power is supreme inside the state because federal law applies only elsewhere
options.misconception: believes federal law stops at state borders

options.text: Sovereignty sits with the courts, which allocate power by issuing decisions
options.misconception: makes the judiciary the source of sovereignty

questions.explanation: Federalism divides sovereignty between two levels that each hold their own powers, with genuine overlap. Treating one level as revocable or as supreme inside its territory inverts the arrangement.
questions.hint: Look for a description that allows both levels power.

questions.topic: Ambiguity of an enumerated list with a reservation
questions.learningObjective: Apply a reserving clause to an unlisted claim
questions.stem: A statute grants the national government three specific powers over interstate sales and then reserves all other powers to the states. A court weighs a claim about regulating purely local sales.

options.text: The claim succeeds, because a grant of related power can be expanded to fill gaps
options.misconception: treats a general grant as covering unlisted local activity

options.text: The claim fails, because the reserving clause leaves the subject to the states
The claim fails, because courts may never read a statute as granting more than it says
options.misconception: misstates the reservation as a general rule on implied power

options.text: The claim succeeds, because the power to regulate sales includes sales made inside one state
options.misconception: assumes a general sales power swallows purely local activity

questions.explanation: The reservation is the textual reason the claim fails, since regulating local sales is unlisted and ungranted. Reading the general power expansively ignores the clause that closes the list.
questions.hint: Begin with the clause that disposes of unlisted powers.

questions.topic: Implied powers and incidental authority
questions.learningObjective: Select the step most clearly tied to the granted power
questions.stem: A programme table lists forms, credit checks, and record retention as steps of a federal loan programme. The statute authorises only the making of loans. Which step is most clearly implied?

options.misconception: reads implied power as a licence to expand the subject

options.text: Levying a surcharge on other lenders to fund the programme
options.misconception: invents new revenue power through implication

options.text: Keeping records of the loans the programme itself makes
Licensing every firm in the state that makes loans
options.misconception: expands programme machinery into a general licensing power

questions.explanation: Record keeping for the loans the statute authorises is a natural and necessary part of making them. The other steps reach well beyond what the enumerated power supports.

questions.topic: Concurrent power and a national floor
questions.learningObjective: Determine the effect of added state requirements
questions.stem: A comparison of national and state workplace safety rules shows identical national minimums and additional state training requirements. Which statement describes the state requirements?

options.text: They are invalid, because only one rule may govern safety in a workplace
options.misconception: assumes duplicate regulation is always unlawful

options.text: They replace the national minimum wherever they apply
options.misconception: treats a floor as a ceiling

options.text: They are valid only if a federal agency certifies them in advance
options.misconception: requires federal approval of stricter state rules

options.text: They operate alongside the national minimum and impose added obligations

questions.explanation: Stricter state requirements may coexist with a national floor because the two do not conflict. The other options assume a single-rule regime or an approval requirement that does not exist.

questions.topic: Scope of the commerce power
questions.learningObjective: Identify the interstate feature in tabulated activity data
questions.stem: An activity table shows a rise of 40 per cent in the volume of goods moving between two states over five years. Which feature most directly supports treating the activity as subject to the commerce power?

options.text: That the goods are continually exchanged between separate state borders
Its effect on employment in the two states where the goods are produced
options.misconception: confuses a downstream effect with the interstate movement

options.text: The total value of the goods, which determines how important the trade is
options.misconception: thinks economic value is the test for commerce

options.text: The number of firms engaged in the trade across the whole country
options.misconception: looks to national totals rather than interstate movement

questions.explanation: The commerce power reaches activity involving movement across state lines, which is what the table records. Economic size or downstream effects are secondary features, not the test itself.
questions.hint: Ask which column shows movement between two states.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Taxing and spending as separate authorities
questions.learningObjective: Identify which entries belong in the collecting column
questions.stem: A finance table separates two federal columns, one listing money paid out and one listing money collected. Which pair of items belongs in the collecting column only?

options.text: Block grants and matching funds paid to states
options.misconception: counts grants as tax collections

options.text: A direct tax on wages and an excise duty on fuel
Cost-sharing payments and construction subsidies to state agencies
options.misconception: mistakes subsidies for levies

options.text: Refunds of overpaid grants and administrative reimbursements
options.misconception: treats refunds of spending as revenue

questions.explanation: Only levies and duties raise money; the rest of the items are payments made out of collected funds. Reading grants or refunds as collections collapses the two columns.
questions.hint: Ask which items bring money in rather than send it out.

questions.topic: Regulating individuals against commanding a state
questions.learningObjective: Identify a rule whose target is a state body

stimulus.body: A regulatory table lists the target of each federal rule: one aims at individuals who sell food, one at a state licensing board, and one at a city's zoning board. The analyst notes that only one entry directs a government body to perform a task.

questions.stem: Reading the table, which entry most clearly involves commanding a state actor?

options.text: The rule aimed at individuals who sell food for profit
options.misconception: sees any rule about a private business as commanding a state

options.text: The rule that sets limits on how food is packaged for sale
options.misconception: sees a product standard as a command to a state officer

options.text: The rule directing the state licensing board to conduct inspections twice a year
The rule that defines which words may appear on a food label
options.misconception: treats labelling rules as commands to state agencies

questions.explanation: A rule that tells a state board what to do binds the state as the regulated party. Rules aimed at private sellers or at products regulate conduct without commanding a state officer.
questions.hint: Ask which entry names a government body as its target.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Express preemption
questions.learningObjective: Apply an express preemption clause to a state requirement
questions.stem: A statute table includes a row for a federal credit reporting statute. The text states that no state or local government may impose requirements on the content of reports for identity theft prevention.

options.text: The federal statute, because the clause expressly displaces state requirements
Both laws together, because nothing in the clause bars a state from adding fields
options.misconception: ignores an express preemption clause

options.text: The state law, unless a court finds an actual conflict between the two texts
options.misconception: reduces an express clause to the conflict test

options.text: Whichever law was enacted first, since the older statute governs
options.misconception: applies a priority rule that the clause replaces

questions.explanation: The clause expressly removes state requirements on the covered subject, so the federal statute governs without any need to find a conflict. The other readings ignore that express displacement.
questions.hint: Ask whether the row needs a conflict to operate.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Federalism as a division of sovereignty
questions.learningObjective: Describe divided sovereignty using grant and reservation
questions.stem: A state constitution table shows that the national government holds enumerated powers while the states and the people hold the remainder. Explain how that arrangement describes the division of sovereignty.

answer.exemplar: The arrangement describes sovereignty as divided rather than located in one level of government: the national government holds only the powers granted to it, the states and the people hold everything else, and no single level is sovereign for all purposes. That is why neither level can claim a general police power over the other.

questions.explanation: The answer should connect the enumerated grant and the reservation to divided sovereignty. Omitting the reservation would present national authority as open-ended and unbounded.
questions.hint: Both the grant and the reservation matter.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Ambiguity of an enumerated list with a reservation
questions.learningObjective: Read a reservation clause against a statutory gap
questions.stem: A table of statutes lists the powers each one grants and notes which powers remain unmentioned. Where a statute grants two powers and reserves the rest, how should a court read the reserved subject?

options.text: As open to national authority, because any gap in a statute invites broader reading
options.misconception: reads gaps as invitations to expand national authority

options.text: As reserved to the states and the people, because the clause itself settles the gap
As open to any level willing to act first on the subject
options.misconception: invents a priority rule for unlisted subjects

options.text: As a question for the courts alone, since the statute says nothing about it
options.misconception: thinks silence removes the issue from the legislature

questions.explanation: An express reservation controls how a court reads the remainder, so the unmentioned subject stays with the states and the people. Filling the gap by implication reverses the clause's purpose.
questions.hint: Ask what the reserving sentence does with the remainder.

questions.topic: Implied powers and incidental authority
questions.learningObjective: Separate the granted power from its implied machinery
questions.stem: A statute table authorises a national programme to issue safety certificates for rail equipment. First identify the granted power, then decide whether a requirement that manufacturers keep testing records falls inside it.

options.text: The granted power is certification; the record-keeping duty falls outside it entirely
options.misconception: treats implied machinery as an independent exercise of power

options.text: The granted power is record keeping; certification is the implied accessory
options.misconception: reverses the granted power and the implied step

options.text: The granted power is certification; record keeping is implied machinery serving it
Both are granted powers, so the manufacturer may refuse either one
options.misconception: assumes each programme step needs separate wording

questions.explanation: The statute grants certification, and keeping records is the natural and necessary means of verifying certified equipment. The reverse reading swaps the granted power for its machinery.
questions.hint: Ask whether the step is necessary to carry out the grant.

questions.topic: Concurrent power and a national floor
questions.learningObjective: State the concurrency rule for state additions
questions.stem: A table comparing two regulatory columns shows the national level requiring one audit a year and states requiring two. Which sentence best expresses the concurrency rule?

options.text: The national requirement is unconstitutional because it occupies the field
options.misconception: treats a federal floor as an unconstitutional takeover

options.text: States may not impose any additional requirement on the regulated activity
options.misconception: reads a floor as a ceiling

options.text: The stricter state rule prevails because states are closer to the activity
options.misconception: invents a proximity principle for supremacy

options.text: States may impose added requirements so long as the national minimum is still met

questions.explanation: Concurrency permits stricter state rules where they do not undercut the national minimum. The other answers assume federal occupation, a ceiling effect, or a proximity rule that does not exist.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Scope of the commerce power
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a cross-border service purchase establishes
questions.stem: A table of services shows that hospital staff in one state treat patients who live in a neighbouring state. Explain what that fact establishes for a claim made under the commerce power.

answer.exemplar: The fact establishes the interstate character of the activity, because the provider and the patients are in different states and the service therefore crosses a state line. It is the starting point rather than the end of the analysis, since a court would still ask whether the regulation is connected to that activity.

questions.explanation: The answer should identify interstate crossing as the key fact and note that further analysis would still be needed. Concluding that any cross-border sale automatically wins overstates the holding.
questions.hint: Focus on where the provider and the patients are located.

It is an exercise of the taxing power against the state
options.misconception: labels a conditional grant as a tax

options.misconception: invents a levy on private patients

options.text: It is not federal action, because the state delivers the care
options.misconception: denies federal power because delivery happens locally

questions.explanation: Conditioning federal payments is the standard way the spending power is exercised, and it reaches states without commanding them. The other descriptions misidentify the power or deny it.

options.misconception: treats market participation as making a party state-related

options.text: The certification requirement for the state agency, because it binds a state body
The factory inspection, because the factory may be licensed by the state
options.misconception: confuses state licensing with a state actor as target

options.text: None of them, because a state body cannot be regulated by federal law
options.misconception: denies that federal law can reach state agencies

questions.topic: Express preemption
questions.learningObjective: Determine the reach of a purpose-limited clause
questions.stem: A statute's text states that no state or local government may require a particular form of identification for a specific purpose. Explain which state measures that clause reaches and which it leaves alone.

answer.exemplar: The clause reaches only state measures that require the same form of identification for the same stated purpose, since those are the ones the text forbids. It leaves alone state measures on other subjects, other identification requirements for other purposes, and general licensing or reporting rules that do not require that particular form.

questions.explanation: The answer should match the clause's words to the state measure rather than to the general field. Reading it as banning all state identification rules ignores the stated purpose limit.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why two columns of powers are both valid
questions.stem: In a table of government functions, the national column lists foreign commerce and the state column lists police power. Which framing best explains why both columns are valid at once?

options.misconception: makes national power dependent on state inaction

options.misconception: invents a priority rule for overlapping authority

questions.topic: Ambiguity of an enumerated list with a reservation
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a reservation clause narrows a local grant
questions.stem: A state statute lists the powers a home rule city may exercise, then adds that anything not listed belongs to the state. Explain how the addition affects a city claim to run a permitting office on its own.

answer.exemplar: The addition operates as a reservation of unlisted authority, so the city would have to point to a listed power authorising the permitting office and could not rely on the power to license buildings merely because cities in other states do so. Home rule language, without a supporting listed power, does not override the reservation.

questions.explanation: A reservation clause narrows what an enumerated grant can support without a listed entry. The answer should note that practice in other states cannot supply the missing authority.

Levelling fines on any company that sells goods below cost

options.text: Negotiating trade agreements on behalf of the nation

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Concurrent power and a national floor
questions.learningObjective: Apply the national floor rule to tabulated standards

stimulus.body: A comparison table sets a national minimum for vehicle inspection intervals at 12 months. Several states inspect at 6 or 9 months, and the table notes that no state rate falls below the national minimum.

questions.stem: Based on the table, what follows when a state inspection interval exceeds the national minimum?

options.text: The national interval is displaced wherever the state rate is more protective
options.misconception: treats the national floor as a ceiling for states

options.text: Only the state interval applies, because states police safety on their own roads
options.misconception: assumes federal standards never bind states

options.text: Both intervals apply, and the state must also satisfy the national minimum
Neither applies, because inspection intervals are purely a state choice
options.misconception: denies that any national minimum constrains states

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Express preemption
questions.learningObjective: Contrast a statute with a clause against one without

stimulus.body: A table of federal statutes includes a row for a statute on vehicle safety containing a clause preempting state requirements on the same subject. A second row records a statute on motor vehicle registration with no preemption language, and the analyst notes that the states still set registration rules.

questions.stem: What does the contrast between the two rows show about how courts should treat the two statutes?

options.text: Both statutes reach state law, because federal statutes always occupy their subject
options.misconception: assumes a federal statute preempts without saying so

options.text: Both statutes leave state rules intact, because preemption needs a court order
options.misconception: requires a court order to give effect to a clause

options.text: The second displaces state rules because it is silent on the subject
options.misconception: treats silence as displacement

options.text: The first displaces state rules on its subject, while the second leaves state rules intact

questions.explanation: The first statute speaks expressly to the subject, while the second says nothing, and silence creates no preemption. The contrast shows that the wording of the statute does the work.
questions.hint: Ask which statute contains a clause at all.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Federalism as a division of sovereignty
questions.learningObjective: Explain how split responsibility illustrates federalism
questions.stem: Comparing two columns of a government index, a reader sees that the national government sets rules for interstate carrier safety while states set rules for local road maintenance. What does that arrangement show?

options.text: That the two levels hold separate powers and also share responsibility for transport
That the national government has taken over all transportation matters
options.misconception: reads shared responsibility as complete federal takeover

options.text: That transportation is reserved entirely to the states until Congress acts
options.misconception: assumes any silence leaves the subject entirely state

options.text: That local maintenance is national policy because the same roads carry traffic
options.misconception: infers federal power from a shared subject matter

questions.explanation: Split responsibility across the two levels is what federalism looks like in practice, with neither level holding every power. The alternatives either overstate federal control or understate it.
questions.hint: Ask whether one level alone could fill both columns.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Ambiguity of an enumerated list with a reservation
questions.learningObjective: Read a general clause against a reservation
questions.stem: A statutory table lists powers granted to the national government, and one row notes that the grant extends to all matters the listed powers touch. How should that row be read?

options.text: As an unlimited grant, since anything touching the listed powers is granted
options.misconception: reads a broad clause as boundless national authority

options.text: As subject to the reservation, since it grants only what the list plus the clause covers
As void, because the listed powers are express and cannot be enlarged
options.misconception: treats enlargement clauses as unconstitutional always

options.text: As a rule that state law prevails whenever the listed powers are touched
options.misconception: assumes a general clause defeats the national grant

questions.explanation: A general clause extends the reading of the listed grants but does not repeal the reservation of everything else. Reading it as unlimited, void, or as favouring state law all misstate the clause.
questions.hint: Ask whether the clause also touches the reservation.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Implied powers and incidental authority
questions.learningObjective: Identify the reading of an incidental equipment step

stimulus.body: An equipment table for a federal mail programme lists buying the mail service, sorting letters, and repairing sorting machines. The analyst marks the third row as an ordinary operational expense rather than a separate exercise of power.

questions.stem: Which reading of the marked row is most consistent with the implied authority described?

options.text: Repairing machines is a separate power that the statute grants on its own
options.misconception: ignores the analyst's classification of the step

options.text: Repairing machines is not covered, because the statute lists only two powers
options.misconception: misses that the statute names one power and implied means

options.text: Repairing machines is machinery for the mail service the statute authorises
Repairing machines is invalid because no statute mentions equipment
options.misconception: requires express mention of every incidental cost

questions.explanation: Repairing the equipment is incidental to the authorised mail service, so it falls within implied authority. The other readings treat machinery as a separate grant or exclude it outright.
questions.hint: Ask whether the equipment serves the authorised service.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Concurrent power and a national floor
questions.learningObjective: Identify which state figure conflicts with a national floor
questions.stem: A programme requirements table shows the national level setting a processing time of 30 days and states setting times of 45 days and 20 days. First identify which state figure conflicts with a national floor, then explain why.

options.text: The 20-day figure conflicts, because it falls below the 30-day national minimum
The 45-day figure conflicts, because it is slower than the national minimum
options.misconception: treats a floor as a ceiling on processing time

options.text: Both figures conflict, because the national rule occupies the field of processing times
options.misconception: assumes floor language displaces stricter state rules

options.text: Neither figure conflicts, because the national rule sets a goal rather than a requirement
options.misconception: treats a statutory minimum as aspirational

questions.explanation: A floor of 30 days means every level must meet or beat it, so a 20-day rule is too fast to comply while 45 days is fine. Treating the floor as a ceiling reverses its meaning.
questions.hint: Ask which figure gives less protection than the minimum.
